transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. Well, what finally pushed me to make this appointment is... I guess it's my work. I manage a health clinic, and I'll sit down to start an EPIC quality report, or I'll be in one of our clinic metrics meetings. Which, honestly, those meetings have gotten so long lately because we just got a new regional director, and he insists on going over every single line item. He used to work in finance, so I think he just loves spreadsheets. My brother is an accountant, actually, and he's exactly the same way—he even color-codes his grocery lists, which I think is a bit much, but... wait, what was I saying? 

Oh, right. So, I go into these metrics meetings with every intention of tracking the information. But within just a few minutes, my mind has drifted so far away. I'll catch myself rereading the exact same numbers on the page over and over, or I'll suddenly realize I completely missed the whole point of the discussion. It's just becoming a real problem.
Have you struggled with this difficulty staying focused on tasks since you were a child, or is this a relatively new development in your life?

Oh, it's definitely not a new thing. Even way back in elementary school, I remember my teachers writing on my report cards that I was bright but careless. My third-grade teacher, Mrs. Higgins, was the one who really started saying that, I think. She always wrote her notes to my parents in this really aggressive red ink. She also had this massive collection of ceramic apples on her desk. Just dozens of them everywhere. I used to just stare at them instead of looking at the chalkboard. Actually, I saw a ceramic apple just like hers at an antique fair last weekend, and it totally brought me back to that classroom. The antique fair was fantastic, by the way, they had all these beautiful vintage Pyrex bowls, the yellow ones with the little daisies on them... 

Wait, sorry, I'm doing it again. What were we talking about? 

Right, childhood focus. So, because I was always drifting off, my mother actually had to sit right there with me at the kitchen table every single night while I finished my homework. If she wasn't sitting there keeping me on it, I would just completely lose track of my assignments. Or I'd actually manage to do the work, but then I'd get to school the next morning and realize I completely forgot my books at home.

Aside from these difficulties with focus and organization, would you say that you have also struggled with feeling physically restless, like you have a motor inside you that won't turn off, or a tendency to act or speak without thinking?

No, I wouldn't say I feel restless like that. I've never been the type to bounce off the walls or just blurt things out. Actually, my husband is the one who can't sit still. He's always pacing around the living room when we watch TV, or he'll start a home improvement project at eight o'clock at night. Just last week, he decided to recaulk the guest bathroom tub while I was trying to watch this documentary on Mount St. Helens. It was fascinating, really—they were talking about how the ecosystem recovered after the eruption, and there were these specific types of lupine flowers that were the first things to grow back through the ash. I've always wanted to grow lupines in my garden, but the soil here is just too clay-heavy. I bought three bags of soil amendment in the spring, but they're still sitting in the garage because... 

Wait, I'm sorry. I lost the thread again. What did you ask me? Something about a motor? But no, I don't have that physical restlessness. It's more just my brain wandering away.
Do you find that you frequently interrupt others when they are speaking or struggle to wait your turn in conversations?

No, I don't think I do that. I'm actually a pretty good listener. Well, I try to be, anyway. My sister, though, she is terrible about interrupting. We'll be on the phone, and she just talks right over me. She called me yesterday while I was at the grocery store, actually. I was trying to decide between the regular organic carrots or those little baby carrots. I know the baby ones are just big carrots cut down, but they're so much easier for snacking. I've been trying to eat more vegetables because my cholesterol was just a tiny bit high at my last physical. My doctor told me to eat more oats, too, so I bought this huge container of steel-cut oats, but honestly, they take so long to cook on the stove. I read somewhere you can make them in a slow cooker overnight, which sounds brilliant. I have this vintage Crock-Pot my mother gave me, it's this wonderful avocado green color from the seventies... 

Oh, gosh, sorry. I did it again. I completely forgot what we were talking about. Did you ask about my sister? But no, I don't really interrupt people or have trouble waiting my turn.
In your daily life, how often do you find that you lose or misplace essential items like your keys, wallet, or phone?

Oh, all the time. It's actually becoming a real problem at work. I'm a health services manager at a clinic, so I really need to be on top of things, but I'm constantly hunting for my work badge, or handwritten notes from the doctors, clinic folders, even the flash drive I just had in my hand two minutes before a meeting. It's so embarrassing because I used to be the organized one. Or at least I thought I was. Speaking of the clinic, we just got these new ergonomic chairs for the front desk staff, and they are incredibly complicated to put together. I spent an hour trying to figure out the lumbar support adjustment on one of them on Tuesday. The instruction manual was completely useless, just these tiny little diagrams that didn't even match the parts in the box. It reminded me of this IKEA bookshelf I bought for my daughter's dorm room when she started college. We were on the floor of her room for three hours, surrounded by all those little wooden dowels. She's graduating next spring, actually, with a degree in environmental science. I'm so proud of her. We're thinking of renting a house near the campus for graduation weekend so the whole family can stay together, but the prices on Airbnb are just astronomical right now... 

Wait, I'm sorry. I lost my train of thought again. What were you asking me? Oh, right, losing things. Yes, my keys, my badge, folders... it's just a constant struggle to keep track of everything I need for the day.
Beyond your social interactions, do you find that you often make impulsive decisions, such as spending money you hadn't planned to or taking unnecessary risks, without considering the consequences?

No, I wouldn't say I'm impulsive like that. I'm actually pretty careful with my money, especially now with my daughter's graduation coming up and trying to figure out that whole Airbnb situation. We really have to budget for that. My husband, though, he's the one who will just buy things on a whim. Like last month, he came home with this massive, top-of-the-line espresso machine. Just out of nowhere! We already had a perfectly good coffee maker, one of those drip ones with the thermal carafe that keeps it hot all morning. I love that carafe. I bought it at this little kitchen supply store downtown that unfortunately closed during the pandemic. It was such a shame, they had the most beautiful imported ceramics. I bought this gorgeous hand-painted serving bowl from Italy there once, with lemons all over it. I usually bring it out for summer barbecues, for potato salad. I make a really good potato salad, the secret is putting a little bit of pickle juice in the mayonnaise...

Oh, dear. I'm doing it again, aren't I? I completely drifted off. You were asking about impulsive decisions, right? No, I'm really not a risk-taker or an impulse buyer. I overthink things, if anything.
